headline: 48-HOUR STRIKE / PARIS STUDENTS DOWN BOOK6.
text:
It is estimated that two thirds of the Paris University Students to-day downed books.

The students in fifteen out of eighteen provincial universities are striking in sympathy.

[The appointment of Professor Georges Scelle, the Principal Secretary of the Minister of Justice and an ardent Socialist, to the Chair of International Law of Paris University, led to fierce encounters between students in the Latin quarter, attended with a long casualty list. Royalist and other anti-Government students resented the appointment as an act of political favouritism, and went in procession to the lecture room and erected barricades, preventing the Professor from lecturing. Later they came into collision with a body of youthful pro-Government students outside the Sorbonne. The police intervened and Communists joined in the meleo. The students scattered, but later reformed and re-engaged the police. Order was eventually restored after 20 had been wounded and 36 made prisoner. Seventy gendarmes were wounded, some seriously.

headline: ARMED ROBBERY. / POLICE TIRE AT A SUSPECT.
text:
An armed robbery was committed at a teashop at Woosung Street, Yaumai, close on midnight yesterday. The mistress of the tea-house, who made a report to the police on after, stated that three me armed with revolvers and daggers rushed into the premises b forcing open the door. headline: GANDE, PRICE & CO.
text:

A decrease of profits but the effecting of improvements which it is confidently anticipated will be the means of increasing the sales and adding to the prestige of the Company was referred to by the Chairman at the annual meeting of Gande, Price and Co., Ltd. Mr. C. H. Lyson presided over the meeting, others present being Messrs. S. C. Pank, Managing Director, C. Bond, Secretary, and the following shareholders.—Leung Yan-po, J. H. Oxberry, D. The Chairman said: Gentlemen, the report and statement of account for the year ending 1924 having been in your hands for the prescribed period, I propose with your permission to take them as read. This is partly due to the extra expenses involved in alterations to our new premises, coolie hire for the removal of goods etc. which cost us approximately $2,000. headline: YEARS AND
text:
TWO YEARS OLD CRIME.

This Morning's

The most striking feature of to-day's Criminal Sessions was the heavy penalty imposed by Mr. J. R. Wood, the new Puisine Judge, on a man convicted of participation in a two years old robbery.

Mr. Wood's first case was that of Mak Sum, charged with robbery on April 15, 1923, at Wong Nei Cheong Village. In the course of her evidence the wife of the robbed man accused the prisoner of having forced into her husband's mouth some poison which had caused his death about twelve days later, but the Crown Solicitor, Mr. Whyte Smith, said that there was some sort of suggestion that the remedies which the man had used had aggravated the injuries.

Although two years had elapsed between the time of the robbery and the arrest of the prisoner, the woman had had no difficulty in picking the man out from thirteen others at the police station. Questioned by Mr. Justice Wood she said that she would only be able to recognise the other men who took part in the robbery "partly per cent," this man she recognised "fully per cent," because he was the one who had tied her husband up. The others had not shown their forms.

The defendant pleaded not guilty this morning but in previous statements he had confessed to participation in the robbery. At the Magistracy he had stated that he had been arrested by a police-man who had told him that he was going to get him employment on a Government launch. This policeman had told him that unless he confessed he would be beaten to death.

The jury found defendant guilty and Mr. Justiçe Wood sentenced him to ten years' hard labour and twelve strokes of the "cat."

headline: PIECEGOODS / “POSITION SOMEWHAT
text:
LEADING EXPERT'S VIEWS.

Unqualified Confidence

Much more reassuring than some of the published statements is the view of the piecegoods'situation, expressed by one of the Colony's experts to a "China Mail" reporter in the course of an interview this morning.

The report was confirmed that, as mentioned in yesterday's issue, the Piecegoods Dealers' Guild has written to the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce asking for co-operation and assistance. With some of the dealers' requests, importers were certainly in sympathy, but it was felt that the waiving of interest on lots not cleared would amount to shouldering charges equivalent to about five per cent. of the cost specified in contracts.

As everybody knows, upcountry conditions have been disturbed for years. Political chaos has been blamed, primarily, for the present deadlock, but it is felt in some quarters that the position has been somewhat exaggerated. During the last two or three years, piecegoods dealers made fairly good profits. Last year, they did not do quite so well, but they did not lose much money. As a result of having several good years, dealers had increased their orders for winter goods to arrive last autumn. Last September, clearances were above average. October was a very bad month on account of the trouble. Between the Canton Government and the Merchants' Volunteers, November and December had been satisfactory.

It was estimated that, from 30 to 40 per cent, of last autumn's arrivals, had not been cleared, mainly through the orders being increased. At this time of the year, winter piecegoods could only be disposed of at a loss. However, on comparing values existing last autumn and now, it was found that in many lines the dealers had bought at prices lower than they were at present. In one or two lines values had slumped.

Clearances of goods ordered for the summer had begun. About 40 per cent. of the Colony's orders had been taken up. At this stage it is not possible to say what will happen to the balance of the orders for the summer as there are a few more months to go. Where dealers did feel the pinch was in the case of uncleared orders of last autumn. Some of the importers were helping their clients out by carrying-over the lots remaining but others had pressed dealers to take delivery. It was also true that some importers had declined to issue delivery orders for summer lots till the autumn lots had been taken up.

Speaking for himself, the gentleman interviewed expressed unqualified confidence in the situation. Admitting that as much as 40 per cent. of last autumn's orders had not been cleared, there were only small lots coming between now and next autumn; probably amounting to about 25 per cent. of last year's total. The total when next autumn comes would be about 60 or 65 per cent. of last year's aggregate. For the whole Colony, even a small percentage represented an enormous sum of money. But if the stocks that would have to be taken up next autumn were only about 60 per cent. of last year's it stood to reason that the dealers—provided they are not unduly pressed in the interval—will be able to take up the whole lot without any difficulty.

The reported failure of the dealer of fifty-eight years' standing had precipitated matters but it was generally agreed that if the principal of the firm had confined his attention to piecegoods and refrained from entering the two fields of speculation in Hongkong which stood for the greatest fluctuations, he would still be in the nature of a gilt-edged constituent to the piecegoods import

ers, if there was such a thing. In consequence of reports in the vernacular press, native bankers had become alarmed and were refusing to finance piecegoods.

In the opinion of the speaker, the so-called impending crisis would be averted if dealers were helped to carry over the balance from last autumn — this being done by some firms with the means. So soon as the summer orders were liquidated, dealers would turn again to winter stocks and by the time next autumn came, they would be faced with a much smaller quantity than last year.

It is expected that the Chamber of Commerce will convene a meeting to discuss the letter from the Piecegoods Guild and that a reply will be sent. But it is impossible to predict what will be done.

headline: PROTEST AGAINST TAXES.
text:
A strife, or indier, a cessation of trade, involving over 40,000 people, is said to be the to start to morrow (Tuesday) as a protest against the taxes being levied and periodically increased by the Canton: civil Government. Eleven different trades are likely to close their doors, it is stated.

I am reliably informed that the strikers intend to march in procession to the Municipal offices where they will present their grievances. headline: "TOOK TO DRINK." / “IRRITATED” BY MISSING HIS BOAT.
text:
FORGED LOST CHEQUES.

That he took to drink "irritated" by missing his boat in Kobe and under its influence cashed cheques which he found in a pocket book lying on the wharf was the plan put forward by an American seaman at the Central Magistracy this morning when charged with forgery.

The accused, who passed under the name of Merjith H. Jones when arrested by the police at the Kowloon Hotel on Tuesday, was charged before Mr. H. R. Butters at the Central Magistracy the following day with being found in the Colony without a valid passport. This charge was only the forerunner of more serious charges. The accused later admitted that his proper name was Richard Edward Dunn.

At the proceedings this morning, there were three charges against the accused in respect of travellers' cheques issued by the American Express Company. The first was forgery of the cheques, the second cashing, them, and the last possession.

The accused pleaded guilty to all three charges and made a statement after the close of the evidence.

The only witness who was called upon to give evidence was Mr. Frank B. Dittman, purser of the s.s. President Cleveland. He stated that the accused, whose name was R. E. Dunn, worked as a night watchman on the vessel and skipped away at Kobe without proper discharge. Witness added that Mr. M. H. Jones was a passenger on his vessel bound for Manila and a report was made at Kobe that his pocket book containing travellers' cheques of the American Express. Company was missing

M. F. C. Vaux, appearing for the American Express Company, said that a report was made to the Company's Shanghai that several cheques issued in favour of Mr. Jones had been stolen or lost. The Company immediately circulated the news to their branches and other concerns. The sum involved in the missing cheques was gold $2,500, of which $1,600 worth of cheques had been found on the accused number had been negotiated, and $450 was still out and may be presented in due course, as Mr. Vaux said that the cheques went from hand to hand a long time like ordinary bank notes before they were presented at the Company's offices. As the American Express Company had taken years to build up the travellers' cheque business, and the loss of a cheque would be damaging to their reputation, Mr. Vaux asked His Worship to take a serious view of the case. He mentioned that Mr. Jones, who was now in Manila, was bringing a claim against the Company in respect of the missing cheques.

At this stage the accused was sentenced to three months hard labour on the first two counts and one month on the last count, the sentences to run concurrently.

The accused made a statement in the course of which he said that he went ashore at Kobe and on coming to the wharf he found that the vessel had already left. Here he picked up a pocket book with the cheques made out in favour of Mr. Jones. Irritated by the fact that he missed the boat, he went and had some drinks and under its influence, commenced to cash the cheques, signing them as M. H. Jones. He added that he had borne a good character in America, and it was only the missing of the boat and the drinks which upset him.

Considering that the American Express Company were faced with claims from various people, Mr. Vaux applied for the restitution of the property found on the accused. These comprised $246.50 in Hongkong currency, an Elgin watch, three gold rings, one gold and jade ring, one piece jade, one silver cigarette case, and some clothing. headline: PIRATES SHOT. / KONGMOON RAID
text:

headline: CHEUNG CHAU NOTES. / GOVERNMENT SCHOOL SPORTS.
text:
The chief event of the week's end was the third annual sports meeting of the Cheung Chau Government School, which passed off very successfully. The weather was all that could be desired not unpleasantly hot and the rain did not fall till late in the evening. There was a large attendance of visitors, most of the foreign residents were present and some of the visitors as well, members of the local Kai Fong and many of the parents and friends of the schoolboys came to shew their interest in the proceedings.

The entrance to the Ball Ground of the C. C. Residents Association was graced with a floral archway surmounted by the School flag. The Volley ball posts were converted into flag poles for the Union Jack and the Chinese flag with wreaths of flowers and streamers of smaller flags Seats and refreshments were thoughtfully provided for the visitors and on a table were displayed the prizes for which the students were to compete. The starting of the 22 events were in the able hands of Inspector Lane and Mr. Lam Pak-to.

The Judges were Messrs. L M. White, Lo Ip, Lau Wai tai, Lai Nan-sang, Tsang Pak-hong, Lo Mo-to, Lau King chi; these gentlemen had a busy time owing to the very close finishes of many of the events.

All the events (with the possible exception of the lantern race which on account of the breeze, difficulty was experienced in lighting the candles, and some finished with their lanterns in flames) were keenly contested, especially the Hill race, Team race, and the Tug of war. After the last event, the visitors and boys gathered round the

prize laden table, where were displayed silver cups, penholders, choosticks, also in kittens, found in pens, fans and other articles of a useful nature. Mr. E. Ralphs then called upon Mrs. Arnold Jones to distribute the prizes to the various winners, whose names were read out by the Headmaster. The School champion, Fung Wa-hin will have his name inscribed for the second time on the cup, having gained that distinction two years ago. Mr. C. G. Alabaster on behalf of Mrs. Arnold Jones (who was presented with a large bouquet of flowers by the school champion) thanked the students for the privilege of having been asked to carry out the pleasant task. Mr. Alabaster also noted the improvement in the arrangements for carrying out the various events and in the keenness among the students, and hoped the future gatherings would be even more successful. Mr. Ralphs after thanking various gentlemen who had worked hard to make the sports a success, called for three cheers for Mrs. Arnold Jones, Inspector Lane, Mr. Whyte, and the judges, cheers were also given for the members of the Kaifong, to those who had contributed to the prizes, fund the visitors. Mr. Alabaster, and the Headmaster. The proceedings having concluded the gathering dispersed.

The Kung-Yik is supposed to report for duty in about five days' time. Mr. and Mrs. Anderson who have been living in Dr. Heanley's house have returned to Hongkong.

headline: CHILD LABOUR LAWS. / FOLLOWING HONGKONG'S
text:
TREATY PORT

No children under twelve are now allowed to work in factories under the jurisdiction of Hongkong but the absence of such restrictions in other Treaty ports has led to severe stricture being passed by Dame Adelaide Anderson who has recently returned to England from China.

Recalling some of her visits to silk factories, cotton mills and match factories, both in Chinese Towns and in the Treaty ports she states:—

"In silk flatures one saw them stirring cocoons in nearly scalding water, in steam-laden air, for nearly twelve hours at a stretch and mostly standing. In cotton-spinning mills, they are working night and day, 6, 7 and 8 years old, at meal times hastily taking food from the rice bowl, with the dust settling on hair, skin,"

clothes and rice, affecting their general health; digestion and lungs.....Too often one had to leave a sick child, with the illness undiagnosed, standing at work, where there is as yet no organised aid for relief. I asked a Chinese woman what became of the little ones of 6 and 7 who enter silk flatures. When they go to work so early they mostly die young was her reply.

Dame Anderson then explained the progress that has been made since the Child-Labour Commission was appointed in June, 1923, by the Executive Council for the International Settlement of Shanghai. The leading manufacturers in the Settlement have assented on the most difficult point—the age of entry for child workers. Also, the Governments of several provinces have assured the Commission of their assistance. Governor Han of Jiangsu Province issued an Ordinance preparing steps for the appointment of a Provincial Child Labour Commission. After Dame Anderson's address Mr. H. G. Simms, late Chairman of the Municipal Council of Shanghai, emphasised the fact that the report of the Child Labour Commission of Shanghai is the most important forward movement towards improving industrial labour conditions in China. Even if there appears to be no immediate solution of the evil of employing children of 10 years of age and under an night work, there is hope that through gradually educating Chinese public opinion labour conditions affecting child work will gradually improve.

The proposals for the regulation of child labour in Shanghai are similar to those already adopted by Hongkong which the S.C.A. in a report earlier in the year said were being met in a whole-hearted manner by local employers. No children under twelve may be employed in factories here and under fifteen they are not allowed to work more than nine hours a day. Employers here are also compelled to give children one holiday in seven. It is anticipated that similar steps to those already taken by Hongkong and contemplated by Shanghai will be taken at Chefoo and Tientsin. In a report on conditions in factories generally at these and other places in China. Dr. Sherwood Eddy stated: "Unrest is growing in the midst of this awful poverty. The workers in the south and central regions and along the railways are learning effectively to strike for better working conditions. Many employers are attempting to keep them contended with their lot. But God forbid that they should accept it."

headline: EUROPEAN ROBBED
text:
RAINCOAT TAKEN BY INDIAN

PAWNED BY "MALAY FRIEND."

Before Mr S. R. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning, a young Indian named A. L. Rumjahn was charged with the larceny of a raincoat, valued at $20, at Wanchai on May 3.

Accused denied the charge of theft, but admitted having pawned the article on behalf of a Malay friend, for whom he acted as interpreter at the pawnshop. His friend had secured lodgings with him for the night, and the next morning asked for assistance to pawn the overcoat as he had no money. He could not find his friend, who was believed to be a seaman.

A pawnbroker, giving evidence, stated that the 'accused came to the shop with a raincoat, which he pawned for $8 and left after putting the money in his pocket. Another man was with the accused, but took no part in the transaction.

Detailing the circumstances leading to the arrest of the accused, Sergeant MacDonald stated that he was on duty at Wanchai on the night of May 3, when a ricsha coolie brought a European passenger to him as he did not know where to take him. After questioning the passenger the latter got down and went aside, as he was feeling unwell, being under the influence of liquor. Accused then came up and asked him (witness) what was the matter with the European and he replied that he was drunk. He (witness) left the scene and on returning about fifteen minutes later found that the European had recovered. He had an idea that the European had raincoat with him when he alighted from the ricsha, and on questioning him he admitted that he had one. On being requested to accompany him to the Police Station to lodge a complaint, the passenger asked him not to worry about it and left in another ricsha. Witness met accused again at 3 a.m. yesterday at Praya East. Questioned regarding the raincoat belonging to the European on the night in question, accused denied having stolen it, but admitted having pawned one on behalf of a Major friend. The pawnshop was pointed out to him (witness) and the article was recovered. He added that he had not been the European passenger again and did not know his identity.

headline: TURNED DOWN. / CONSTITUTIONAL REFORM REJECTED.
text:
HOME DECISION

News has been received that the Secretary of State for the Colonies does not consider the time's opportunity for the introduction of Constitutional Reform as advocated by the 1,500 Hongkong residents who signed the petition and the matter is not likely to be taken further for some considerable time.

A “China Mail” representative made enquiries this morning as to when a meeting was to be convened on the subject in view of a recent statement of the late President that when a reply was received to enquiries sent home resolutions would be put to a meeting which would be duly advertised.

He was informed that Col. John Ward, M.P., who had been asked to state how the petition stood which had been sent in the name of the Colony's residents, had replied that the Secretary of State for the Colonies had been communicated with and had

expressed the opinion that the time was not "opportunes" for the introduction of such measures as the petition advocated. Col. John Ward was not "therefore disposed to press the matter in the House and it was not likely that the Association would proceed further." In the matter at any rate for some considerable time, the "China Mail" man gathered.

The petition referred to was circulated in the Colony and copies of it and other information about the Colony, it may be recalled, were sent to every member of the House of Commons. Several Parliamentarians known to be specially interested in this part of the Empire were communicated with. Through some technical defect the petition was referred back and before it could come up again the Coalition Government was dissolved. Since then no further news was received until the reply from Col. John Ward came to hand as to the attitude of the Secretary of State for the Colonies. The exact nature of the desired changes in constitution were not actually formulated in the petition which was sent Home, but the object in sending the petition was to ensure that Parliament should be better acquainted with the position in Hongkong, it being the belief of many that the authorities at Home were genuinely in sympathy with the claims of the community and that it is practicable scheme of reform could be found they would find it. The unfavourable reply which has now been received, however, does away effectively with any hope of support being received from the Government and in the belief that the Government with its large majority would effectively quash any private member's measure it is apparently the intention of those in interested to drop the subject for the present.

headline: MARTIAL LAW. / CRITICAL CANTON POSITION.
text:
GENERAL STRIKE?

CHAN KWING-MING COMING BACK?

Once more General Chan Kwingming's name is mentioned in connection with Kwangtung politics. This time he is only making a mild attempt to regain a footing in the province instead of striking for complete conquest.

Martial law was declared this morning by the Yunnanese mercenaries in the East Suburb, where soldiers are on guard in public streets with fixed bayonets.

General Hsu Shung-chi, the Kuomintang general, is reported to be coming back to Canton to make a grand effort to stem the tide of anti-Communistic aggression and to expel the non-

In addition to the threatened political upheaval, Canton may face a general strike. The Yunnanese have declared that they will protect the electricity and water works from unruly strikers.

Gradually the process of converting Canton into a mercenary capital is being carried out. I am told that even the Cement Works at Honam, formerly Dr. Sun's headquarters, are now guarded by the Yunnanese.

headline: BUSINESS WITH BRAZIL. / CONGESTED PORTS.
text:
Advices from Sao Paulo emphasise the fact that special caution should be exercised at the present time in dealing with this part of Brazil. The port of Santos is in "a deplorable state of congestion, and merchandise will be held up" for months. In view of this many local importers have repeated orders for goods to be sent to Rio de Janeiro, with the result that the port is also becoming congested. Due to this duplication of orders, it is probable that much merchandise will be refused.

In the second place, owing to the prolonged drought and the intense heat experienced this summer, water has become scarce and the Light and Power Company is in serious difficulties. Power is being rationed, and factories will be closed a certain number of days per week. One factory alone has dismissed over a thousand workmen, and others are following suit. The outcome will undoubtedly be serious labour trouble in the near future, and there are already rumours of strikes and revolution.

The outlook is far from pleasant. There is political agitation in the north, with the possibility of Federal Government intervention with troops. Agitation is already commencing with regard to the election of the next President.

headline: PROGRESS OF PALESTINE
text:
Sir Alfred Mond summarising to newspaper correspondents in Jerusalem his impressions of his three weeks' stay in Palestine, said that he found very noticeable improvement in the general political situation and more understanding by all concerned of the position. He ascribed this to the better relations between Jews and Arabs. The financial position of the Government was much better than four years ago. Some of the industries introduced by Jewish money and effort might be regarded as "large industrial capitalistic enterprises," such as the salt works at Athlit, the oil and soap works. "Shemen," the flour mills, and the Nesher cement works, all at Haifa. He was gratified with the introduction of the new industries, such as silk, tanneries, furniture, and textiles, in all of which the latest machinery was used by people who knew their business. The orange industry, he said, was capable of very great development; and he was confident that Palestine could grow first-class tobacco. He saw a great future for dairying, poultry farming, and vegetable-growing. There was no reason for doubts as to the success of agriculture, in view of the fact that it was possible to raise in Palestine three crops a year on irrigated land.

Sir Alfred also spoke of the mineral resources of the Dead Sea, a matter which, he said, was arousing considerable interest because of phosphate and other deposits.

headline: RUSSIAN PRODUCTS.
text: A number of interesting facts and figures are to be found in a New Year's speech by Finance Commissioner Sokolnikov, delivered at Leningrad. Before the war Russia, according to Sokolnikov, produced 576,000,000 pounds of cotton. In 1919 cotton production fell to 48,000,000 pounds. Last year this figure rose to 236,000,000 pounds; and next year a production of 396,000,000 pounds is anticipated. Despite this increase in the Russian cotton production, Sokolnikov declared that imports of American cotton next year would exceed pre-war figures in order to keep up with the growing requirements of the textile industry. Last year Russia produced over 400,000 tons of sugar against almost 1,200,000 tons before the war. Next year it is hoped to raise this production to 666,000 tons. Sokolnikov declared that the Soviet Government spends three-quarters as much on education as on military needs, whereas the Tsarist Government spent three times as much on the army and navy as on education.

headline: GOLDEN DREAMS.
text:
Nobody can have read the report of the launching of the Changte at the Kowloon Dockyard yesterday without a feeling of pride. That the order for such a vessel as the Changte should have been placed in Hongkong is in itself a trihute to the Colony's growing importance as a shipbuilding centre, since Australian owners desiring an ocean-going steamer for a highly competitive route must obviously turn to the best market for their requirements. Gratifying as the launching of the Changte is in this respect, it is even more gratifying, however, as evidence that the Colony not only possesses the labour for such work but also possesses that even greater asset, the technical skill. Therefore it is no idle dream to look forward to the day when Hongkong dockyards will turn out mail liners for the great ocean trades—when the Colony will have become the Clydebank of the Far East. Those will be great days, but they are yet far off, and it behaves us, before we are carried away on the wings of hope, to take stock of

our position. There have not been wanting signs during the past few years that the golden future which is almost within our grasp will not be won without the greatest vigilance. Already production costs are ominously high—we were told during a recent strike that moulders' wages were perilously near the Home level—and unless labour takes the same view they may easily become prohibitive. There is no need to dwell upon what that will mean. The very reasons that led to the placing of the order for the Changte in Hongkong will lead to such orders being placed elsewhere. Commerce has only one standard—the strictly practical. Therefore if we are to win the favours of commerce we must keep to the strictly practical. Hongkong to-day possesses the money, the brains and the labour to compete with other parts of the world. The brains and the money will always be ready to play their part. The future therefore rests with the workmen. Labour cannot be made to see that fact too clearly for its own welfare and for the general prosperity of the Colony. That as much as anything is the moral of the launching of the good ship Changte.

headline: SUN'S OLD. SHIP.
text:
RENAMED IN HIS MEMORY

From Our Own Correspondent.)

In memory of Dr. Sun Yat-sen, it has been decided to rename the cruiser Wing Fung after him.

According to the vernacular papers, a ceremony attended by the leading officials of the Kuomintang was held on board the cruiser when it was given the new name of Chung San—Dr. Sun having been known as Sun Chung san, to the Chinese, in the latter part of his career.

It is believed that the Wing-Fung was one of the Northern Cruiser squadron that broke away from Peking when Dr., Sun came to Canton to organise his Constitutional Government. The late Admiral Ching Pek-kwong led the squadron South and he was later assassinated in Canton. Admiral Ching's statue now stands on Dutch Folly.

When General Chan Kwingming delivered his coup in June, 1922, Dr. Sun fled to the Wing Fung which bombarded Canton and was subsequently bottled up, off Shameen, for some weeks. The other ships in the squadron gradually deserted Dr. Sun but the Wing Fung remained as his flagship to the last.

Presumably Dr. W. V. M. Koch was correct when he inferred that the Government's reply to the Sanitary Board's typhoid resolution could be taken as having been carefully thought out—the Principal Civil Medical Officer being hardly "likely to write a minute upon such an important subject without giving the matter the most careful thought. Therefore when Dr. Addison urged the necessity for the "gradual improvement of the sanitary conditions generally," we may read the remark to mean that in his considered opinion the present methods are anything but satisfactory. The public did not of course require to be told that there is urgent need for reform—they have known that for many

years now—but Dr. Addison's remark is interesting as one of the few official admissions that much has yet to be done before the Colony can think about its sanitary problems without anxiety. Apart from the primitive nature of many of the methods still employed, apart too from the confusion inevitable through the lack of a board of health, much of the present trouble can be traced to the serious under-staffing of the Sanitary Department, especially as regards the number of men for the inspecting of food, etc. Compared with a Home town of similar size, Hongkong is woefully backward in this respect. The fact has long been known but so far little has been done to remedy the defect. The Sanitary Department undoubtedly performs its work with model efficiency, and this no doubt is why the Government persists in that laissez faire policy Dr. Koch denounced at Tuesday afternoon's meeting of the Sanitary Board. "But such a policy, while it may serve for the moment, is simply trifling with the community's welfare. It is taking no account of the future and the unknown dangers that lie ahead. Nature has a nasty way of resenting such neglect. She will allow liberties to be taken with impunity and then—she will strike with a terrible hand. Hongkong has learnt that bitter lesson in the past. Unless the Government bestirs itself the Colony will learn it again in the future.

The former has resulted in quarrels often ended in death, and left the world considerably worse for their being. The modern has certainly added to the gaiety of nations; done not a little to keep minds occupied and to enlarge interest that otherwise would have remained stagnant and perhaps gone into less wholesome grooves. Already Crossword puzzles have done much to extend knowledge in every grade of thought. It is not merely that one thinks of cat as the equivalent of an animal expressed in three letters. headline: Arms Searches.
text: It is possible to feel sympathy for both those whose duty it is to be searched, and those called upon to be searched. If the latter can only be got to see that the duty is, so to speak, a double-edged one, matters may be simplified. The honest person should have no hesitation in allowing a search to take place, and should certainly not resist. On the other hand the authorities should so conduct their search as to make it as acceptable as possible. It should be done “in decency and in order”; if possible, not in full view of others, but to one side of a thoroughfare or place. It should not be made to appear that certain classes only are liable to be searched, but that the whole community is made responsible. This fact should be broadcast. Exceptional diseases demand exceptional remedies. These sudden searches have already proved their effectiveness. They should be continued.

headline: LABOUR TROUBLE. (Reuter's Service.)
text: While employers and trade unions in the shipbuilding industry have agreed to begin a joint enquiry into the serious plight of shipbuilding, a less conciliatory spirit marks the engineering industry, whose troubles are equally serious. The executives of forty engineering trade unions assembled in London to consider the position as regards their demand for an increase in wages of twenty shillings weekly, which the employers have already refused, were astonished to receive a communication from the Employers' Federation declaring the position and prospects of the industry had worsened as the result of foreign competition. A drastic remedy was essential. Therefore they were proposing to increase the weekly hours from forty-seven to fifty for day time, and fifty-two and a half for night time, with modification of overtime rates. The letter suggested the employers' unions will jointly urge the Government to approach Continental competitor nations with the view to some arrangement under a Treaty to secure better working conditions on the Continent. This has greatly disturbed labour trade union opinion, which believes the attitude of the engineering employers, foreshadows a general movement for longer hours.

headline: FASCISM'S SPREAD.
text:
It is the natural boast of the rulers and founders of what is known as Fascism, that it has spread abroad and that the movement is to be found in forty countries including Conservative England. On the 23rd of March last, the Fascisti celebrated the sixth anniversary of the foundation of their party. It was first known as Fascio di Combattimento and at the inaugural meeting presided over by the now recognised high priest of the craft—Benito Mussolini—held in a small back room in Milan, there were present 200 adherents. In 1921 the Fascio di Combattimento became the Fascist Party of Italy, and thirty Fascist members were returned to Parliament. Like most movements that have come to birth and remained active, the original ideas or rules which governed the organisation are little heard of today. The 1919 programme contained such things as the abolition of the Senate, the introduction of woman suffrage, partial workers' control in industry, a heavy progressive tax on capital, sequestration of religions properties, nationalisation of all factories for arms and explosives, and other aims that might readily be described as purely Sociistic. Whatever may be said against the movement, the fact that it has existed so long is not to be despised, whilst the fact also that it has made Italy a country to be reckoned with, has also to be noted. Outside Italy the Fascist

movement is not likely to take any great hold on the minds of the people in the country in which it has found a temporary resting place.

headline: Assassination.
text: The Continent is the cock-pit of Europe. They grow bitter weeds there, and the result is death and the thing that leads to death—war. As the number one Robot said—"Read History." Why certain parts of Europe should breed the pestilential trait of mind to be found in unholy and senseless anarchy no one seems to know. It may be that minds brood more deeply than in the colder clime of Britain where the motto might be said to be—"Be slow to anger." Why should there be a desire to "remove" Mr. Austen Chamberlain, the British Foreign Secretary? What object would be gained in taking away a life which it would be generally admitted, is and has been, stainless? There is no sensible answer to such a question. The present Government has seen fit to reverse its predecessor's arrangement with the Russian Soviet Government. It might be said that the electorate gave it a mandate to do so. It may be that certain elements in Russia see in this a just cause for "direct action." Such a line of thought is beyond understanding. That it exists on the Continent is obvious. That Governments are not able to guard against it has already been proved. All the more reason then why the persons of those who serve the nation so ably, conscientiously and well should be guarded with the utmost care; more especially when the exercise of their duties call them to "foreign parts."

A piece is also always borne about by many in their pockets or purses, as a prophylactic against witching. Not so very long since either the farmers used to have whipstocks of rowan tree wood—rowan tree-gads they were called, —and it was held that, thus supplied, they were safe against having their draught fixed, or their horses made restive by a witch. headline: Open-Air Music.

Tuesday is band night and whilst officers of the regiment are at dinner the band below supplies that which makes a bad dinner seem good and a good dinner seem better. No one is likely to suggest that the officers of the garrison be deprived of what we imagine is a privilegele pleasure. But the time has arrived when the community should have free and unfettered opportunity of listening to the band other than on a narrow pavement and through iron bars. Is it too much to suggest that the much-appreciated experiment of last summer be repeated and that the community be once more given the opportunity—in the cool of the day—to hear music, which a famous poet assures as "vibrates in the memory"? We do not seek to add to the labours of the members of the band. They should not be neglected in any scheme that is brought forward. What we plead for now is a development of the scheme initiated last summer. What about a Public Band Committee?

headline: MAN OF MILLIONS
text:
The “Literary Digest” in a review of Mr. Doheny's career says that in Mexico he gathered in the oil lands until he had the control of no less than 1,400,000 acres on the east coast in the neighbourhood of Tampico, and he developed them that Tampico is said now to be the second port on the American continents for the value of its export. He managed this by his liberality to the President of Mexico to whom he made an advance of $25,000,000. He has covered his vast bailiwick in Mexico with railroad tracks, pipe lines, wagon roads, nests of monster storage tanks, refiners, pumping stations and houses for employees, and runs a fleet of fifty tank steamers all of them busily engaged in making dollars for Doheny.

According to the "Digest," Mr. Doheny is one of America's Dollar Emperors of whom there are three. The other two are John D. Rockefeller and Henry Ford, and which of the three has the greatest number of millions to his credit is not known. Mr. Hoheny is the "herg" of the Tenpot Dome scandal; and his name has been much before the world of late. It is therefore worth while to inquire what manner of man he is. To judge from his name—Doheny—and his description he must be of Irish extraction. His eyes are said to be of the clearest blue that was ever seen, and his voice is full of winning tones which would coax the birds off the tree, both of which are characteristic of the Irish.

He started in Fohd du Lac, Wisconsin where he received a good-high school education, but refused to settle down to any steady occupation. The world was his oyster and with his own two hands he would go forth and open it. He had the idea of discovering a gold mine, or a silver mine somewhere—even copper coal, would not be ignored—so he

set out as a prospector. He wandered about for many years and found nothing, till at last he was compelled to face the problem of getting some work to do in order to keep the wolf out of his empty pockets. What he got was a little road-side school house in the small town of Kingston. New Mexico, where the salary was proportionate to the size of the school. This was in 1887. The district around was unsettled, and the haunt of horse-thieves, cattle-rustlers and bad men generally, so E. L. D. became a leader in the local vigilance committee, and went man-hunting all over the Rio Grande Valley. The bad men sent him notice to quit; otherwise something unpleasant would happen to him, but he paid no attention. Then, when going along the street one morning, a gunman, who was hiding behind a dry goods box on the other side, emptied the magazine of a Winchester rifle at him. Sixteen shots in all were fired and they all missed. Probably the marksman had been strengthening his nerves with a little strong drink. Empty handed E.L.D. crossed the street and took his assailant prisoner, and later on had him locked up for a few years.

headline: PENNILESS AT FORTY.

But the wanderlust was still strong within him so he was next found with a chum in a little hotel on the outskirts of Los Angeles in their usual condition of "stony-broke." They had only ten cents between the pair of them and after a debate, decided to spend the money in grapes, as being the cheapest and most wholesome thing they could get. By this time, E.L.D. was forty years old and the elusive fortune seemed further away than ever. Just them a negro with a cartload of redish earth passed the door. He sampled the stuff and finding it greasy enquired where it came from. Then the two of them had a look at the place and thought there might be oil there.

There were no funds for boring machinery so they started in with "pick and shovel to dig a hole, and" by the time they got thirty feet deep they "struck oil," a commodity in which E. L. D. had not been previously interested. They so manipulated this strike that it netted them millions and filled the pockets of the landowners all round. Here's cheer! Forty years of age and only ten cents between two, and in a hand's turn they were multimillionaires.

Next Edward L. Doheny went definitely in for oil. He travelled through California securing possession of a large number of properties which promised to be oil bearing, and then turned his attention to Mexico.

He owns the finest private yacht that was ever built, the Casiana which takes thirty-eight officers and men to handle. He has a great mansion in Los Angeles with conservatories and sanatorium, and in order to secure that he had good neighbours he bought up all the other fine houses around. He gives liberally to causes in which he takes an interest and to his political party. He financed the Irish in their war against the British, and is at present building a new Catholic Church in Los Angeles which may cost him up to a million, while he also gives liberal help in connection with public disasters and hospitals. With all this wealth at command he shows no signs of retiring to enjoy it, having probably learned the secret that happiness is not to be found in the wealth but in the world.

headline: MOSCOW'S COFFIN.
text:
COMMON THING OF GLASS AND TINT

SUN YAT-SEN'S FAMILY

The much-heralded coffin which the Soviets offered as a permanent repository for Dr. Sun Yat-sen's remains has turned out to be a thing of plain glass and tin, writes the Peking correspondent of the "N. C. Daily News" under date April 2. It is stated that it will not be used. Comrade Karakhan promised to have a coffin made in Moscow like Lenin's, which was of bronze and crystal glass, but the one that arrived some time ago had only a thin coating of bronze, the remainder being of tin, with an ordinary glass top cover.

The Peking Union Medical College reported these facts to Dr. Sun's family and the Kuomintang party leaders, after examining the coffin. As the College had embalmed the body of Dr. Sun and had guaranteed its preservation for something like 150 years under certain conditions, the College examined the coffin from Moscow to see that it did not defeat his aim. It was then that the real composition of the Moscow product was brought to light, as also the fact that it contained several holes, evidently caused in transportation, although it is stated that it is by no means new.

These revelations have been most painful to the family and persons close to the deceased leader, for in China a coffin is considered to be of supreme importance in attesting the honour in which the dead are held, and it is felt that Dr. Sun Yat-sen's memory has already suffered by this evidence of disrespect. headline: That Word "Hand!"
text:
In spite of his schemes for profit sharing Lord Leverhulme was not a believer in joint committees of masters and workers. "There must," he said, "be a captain in everything." He hated the word "hand," however, and one of his most recent utterances was that "the word does more damage to the relationships between master and man than any question of higher or lower wages. "Safety First" in business is to

His early career is a record of application, to hard work, which enabled him in ten or twelve years to rise from errand-boy to owner of a grocery business which five years later he was able to sell for £60,000. With the help of his Brother he then founded a soap factory at Warrington. From controlling an output of 20 tons a week his business has grown to such an enormous extent that he controlled at the time of his death a very great part of the world's soap market and owned factories on the Continent, in the United States, Canada, Australia, South Africa and Japan. His business also controlled the sources of supply of the raw material with huge coconut plantations in the Solomons and in other Pacific Isles and with palm-oil forests in tropical Africa. His firm owned whole groups of islands in the South Seas the object being the maintenance of a constant supply of coconuts for the copra which was turned into Sunlight Soap.

text:
[By NORMAN C, McLOUD.]

In climbing a pole does a vine twist to the left or to the right?

To the left or to the right? To Nature Lovers the question is full of interest; and since most of PB find pleasure in the curious workings of natural laws the answer is worth the seeking. Close observation reveals striking individuality in the twining habits of plant growth.

Some vines twist to the right after the fusion of the hands of a clock in circling the dial. Others turn to the left and seem to grow backwards. In most cases the habit is fixed throughout an entire group or family. In others there is variation, even among vines of close kinship.

Climbing Vines are interesting forms of growth, which depend on outside help for their meats of support. In fact, that they may realize their ambition to rise in the world they avail themselves of any upright object available, whether growing or otherwise. The support may be the trunk of a tree, the post of a fence or the wall of a building. Any object, according to the chants to climb is welcome, to the climbers.

More Than One Way To Climb. In establishing themselves on their supports the vines have notions of their own as to the ways and means to be adopted. Most climbers attach themselves by coiling. With others the contact with the tree or post is effected by means of adhesive disks, as in the case of the widely distributed Virginia Creeper. Another type of vine attaches itself by means of tendrils which are thrown out in all directions to take hold of anything in reach. In this latter class are the gourd and the grape; the grasping tendrils of which are familiar to everyone.

Whether twinning or otherwise fastened to its support, the vine has a definite object in view when the upward journey is undertaken. To the Nature student the climbing habit is essentially utilitarian. Ascending growth is necessary to the fulfillment of the vine's life mission of displaying its flowers to the flitting bees and offer the seeds to the winds and the birds. In discussing the subject for the American Nature Association, Dr. Frederick Brooks has pointed out peculiarities in which most of us will find suggestions for surprise breeding observations of our own.

The case of the climbing bean of the home garden is one of the striking examples of individuality in vines. This form of vegetation always twines to the right. Wild or tame, sturdy or poorly nourished, in sunlight or in shade, the bean twists in the one direction. No allurement of nature seems to influence it to the left. The bean rises in a right-hand spiral with a persistence not to be overcomed. The hop vine is similarly constant This plant the growth is always to the left, and Dr. Brooks reports that his observation has never revealed an exception to this dominant rule. Among the right hand twines we find the climbing buckwheat, dodder, h 线 and Dutchman's pipe. Among those twisting to the left are the wild yam and the Japanese honey-suckle. With any of these plants the amateur will find an interesting field of experiment in trying to force the growth in the opposite direction. Efforts of this character develop the full stubbornness of the vines and bring ultimate failure of the human effort. In this respect the vines seem to know what they want and to defy the efforts of mankind to divert them from their course.

Legend Of A Great Bridge. Shortly after attention is riveted on the Washington shore for Castle Rock which Lewis and Clark called Beacon Rock looms up. It covers thirteen and a half acres and can be seen for miles. No wonder Lewis and Clark used it for a landmark. The Indians, too, play their part in the stories of this inspiring river. In one place, on the Washington side is seen the north abutment of the "Bridge of the Gods." The legends say that at one time the great stream was spanned at this point by a natural bridge, but Mt. Hood and Mt. Adams quarrelled and in their rage the great bridge was shattered. Still more romantic is the story that an Indian brave from the Oregon side married an Indian maiden from the Washington

side in spite of the opposition of their tribes. As they started across the bridge to his home they were pursued by her disappointed suitors and kinsmen. Hardly had they reached safety than the bridge fell, carrying with it their advancing enemies. At any rate the bridge fell and formed rapids in the river.

Indians play a prominent part in legends of this river. Castle Rock, 1,140 feet high, whose summit has only recently been sealed by the white man, was an Indian lookout, and Memalooose Island was used by the Indians for many years as a burying ground, the dead being placed in pine huts. On this island is the grave of Vicor Trevitt, a pioneer river man whose wish was to be buried with the Indians. "If there should be such a thing as a resurrection," this sceptic said, "I will take my chance with the Indians."

Fish wheels in operation gather the sufficient salmon in many places and there are the Dalles and the falls of Cadillac—thirty feet high—and the locks which lift the boats to the level of the Middle Columbia. All these are a part of the enjoyment of a trip on the Columbia. Above the Dalles the river becomes unnavigable, caused by balastic formations and this stretch is a favourite spot among the Indians, many of whom live near by. During the fishing season they can be seen far out on the rocks, speaking salmon which are dried in the sun and used as food. This mighty river with a flow of over 1,800,000 cubic feet of water every second — greater than either the Mississippi or St. Lawrence—fed by overlasting snow fields and glaciers, winds its way through the Pacific North-west and at the mouth the tide reaches in for one hundred and fifty miles. Its crags, cascades, cataracts and falls are worth going many miles to see. If Neolithic man chose this water way to enter this continent he is to be congratulated on his good taste and forenight. At any rate present-day man can see no more picturesque river.

Vines are not alone in the peculiar characteristics of twining growth. The spiral tendency is definitely established for the trees as well. In many species of forest growth we find trunks that are as strikingly twisted as the vines which may have encompassed their trunks. In tree growth, of course, the spiral has less emphasis, but it is none the less noticeable and impressive.

On some trees the twisting habit manifests itself even in the development of the barb, and examination will show the outside covering of the trunks winding their way toward the top in consistent aspiration. The real manifestation of this ch: aeteristic, however, is found by the man engaged in splitting a trunk for firewood. In work of this kind the labour is often doubled by the difficulty of separating the twisted fibres of the wood—an experience with which every rail-splitter or woodcutter is familiar.

Constancy of direction is not found in the twisting tendency of all trees, but there are several species in which the habit of growth is practically uniform, and in which all specimens will show the same characteristics of twining to either right or left. This is especially true in the case of the chestnut. The wood of this tree is allogetner apt to be marked by twisting fibres, and it has been found that in most cases the direction of the twist is toward the left. Specimens with the right-hand twining of the grain are declared to be comparatively scarce. In the case of the common beech the tendency is the same, and like the chestnut, these trees produce spirals of left-hand twist. This is also true of the staghorn sumac, that widely distributed tree of the brilliant red berries and scarlet foliage widely scattered throughout a large portion of the United States.

When it comes to the growth of tendrils the vines show fine disregard of the law of spirals. There is no sense of direction in a tendrill, as these offshoots of the parent stem adapt themselves to the convenience of the moment in choosing their direction of growth. Reaching forth to find a twig on which to fasten themselves, the tendrill of a grape or hop vine will extend themselves in the direction of being the best foothold, right left up down or otherwise. In this form of nature study the material is easily reached, even by those of us who live in crowded cities. Rambles in parks, gardens and wood lands will open the way for an interesting field of observation and teach us many of the secrets of nature in the arrangement of her products. The study requires little or not effort and will be found well worth the required attention.

headline: ANOTHER OPERA? / PHILHARMONIC SOCIETY ACTIVITIES.
text:
COMMITTEE TO DECIDE

It is probable that Hongkong will have another light opera this winter if the feeling of those attending a special meeting of the Philharmonic Society held at the Cathedral Hall yesterday afternoon is at all representative. The meeting considered the replies received to the questionnaire circulated to members.

Mr. S. Collett took the chair in the absence of Sir Claud Severn and after explaining that the policy of the Society was indefinite in many respects he called upon Mr. Mills, the Hon. Secretary, to address the meeting on the subject of the replies received to the questionnaire.

Mr. Mills said that 45 replies had been received out of 120 forms circulated. Twenty-eight specified a preference for light.opera alone, 13 were for one opera and one concert and four for the confining of the society's activities to concerts only. Although preference had been so indicated, 34 of those who replied were ready to participate in whatever policy was adopted and 11 failed to express an opinion on the point.

The Chairman then tabled a proposal by Mr. Mills and seconded by Mr. G. H. Piercy, that the meeting was in favour of the production of one light opera and at least one concert during the forthcoming season.

This was eventually carried unanimously, although Mr. Gillingham expressed the opinion that as Mr. W. G. Wheeler was leaving the Colony the question of a producer should be decided first.

The meeting was thrown open for a short time for the purpose of receiving suggestions as to a suitable opera to produce, those receiving most support being Iolanthe and Merrie England, Pirates of Penzance had many supporters but it was thought that this was outside the scope of the Society. Les Cloches de Corneville was suggested by a member but received no support, nor did the Maid of the Mountains, one of the suggestions sent in. Other suggestions sent in were for the production of Cyrano de Bergerac, Rebel Maid, Highwayman Love and Veronique.

On the proposition of Mr. Penny, seconded by Mr. Gillingham, the matter of the choice of an opera was left to be decided by the Committee.

Election of officers followed, Miss Mow Fung being appointed to the post of treasurer and Mr. Gillingham, Honorary Secretary with Mr. Jefford as Assistant.

headline: TRAVELLER'S PERSONAL
text:
DEBATE IN HOUSE.

BROADENING THE BASIS OF

In the House of Commons, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Winston Churchill, announced that the present scale of the silk duties was not in all details the absolute final.

"Immediately the Budget resolutions had been finally passed, he would begin discussions with the real and artificial silk trades and associations."

The Government merely asked the House to assent to the principle of a silk tax, after which all parties, including the Government, would be free to revise the present scale.

Mr. Churchill said it was impossible to tax real silk and leave artificial silk free which would cripple and destroy the natural silk industry. Both must be treated equally. This was attempted in the proposed scale which, however, was subject to revision.

He announced regarding made, up importations that there would be a reasonable personal allowance for travellers in order that no appreciable inconvenience might be suffered by the travelling public.

Provisional agreement with the trade had been reached regarding made-up importations containing only a proportion of silk on a basis of a lower duty when the silk content did not exceed twenty per cent. and a possibly still lower duty for articles containing only the smallest proportion of silk.

The actual Reduced rate had not yet been fixed. Mr. Churchill said that silk taxes were an essential part of the Government's policy of broadening the basis of taxation.

Mr. Churchill in conclusion said he did not see why the tax on a raw material like silk should be considered monstrous when all the Governments for years past had taxed sugar.

Sir Alfred 'Mond (Labour), opposing the duties, said that when he was recently in the East he had been filled with alarm on going into the Bazaars in Syria and elsewhere to see British textile goods rapidly being replaced by goods from Japan, Czechoslovakia and Italy.

Labour amendments postponing the operation of the silk duties from July 1, to December 1, and omitting the customs duty on artificial silk were both rejected, and at the report stage of the Budget resolutions authorising the customs and excise duties on silk were carried by 330 to 166 votes, thereby completing the report stage of all the Budget resolutions, after which the Finance Bill founded thereupon was introduced by Mr. Churchill, and read for the first time.

(To the Editor of the China Mail)

Sir.—In reference to your leaderette on the above subject, it may interest you to know that confirmation of the gist of the statements made in the circular referred to, could be easily obtained, together with definite facts, figures, from the musters, officers and engineers on board the coasting and river steamers sailing out of Hongkong.

The crew are engaged and paid by one of the numerous "owners" or one of his minions, and though they sign on the articles for the wages agreed upon, after the seamen's strike, between the Seamen's Union and the owners, it is an absolute certainty that not in more than half a dozen companies, at the most, do any of the crew get what they sign on for.

In the U.K., according to the Merchant Shipping Act, the crew are paid by the master, and woe betide any master, or owner, who might try to play tricks with the portage—or wage—bill.

It is not within, my knowledge that any local Act has ever been passed which negatives that clause in the Home Merchant Shipping Act, but, H.K. fashion, a custom has grown up, by which the master has nothing whatever to do with either paying or engaging the crew.

One reason is that the crew are paid monthly, though the articles are for six months. Every month, therefore, each member of the crew signs for his wages as an advance. He is actually paid anything from 10 to, say, 80 percent, of his wages, and signs a receipt in full. He dare not do otherwise. Should the shipping master ask any questions when the crew are signing off at the end of the six months, this receipt would be produced.

The only remedy at all possible, is to enforce the M. S. Act, and make the master responsible for the engaging and paying of the crew—if not the engagement, at least all payments. Incidentally it may, or may not, be news, that there are many Europeans paid on exactly the same system. They sign on for the full wages, and as the price of keeping their job, have to hand back an agreed amount to somebody at the office. I am referring to Chinese owners, and even then, there are still a few who do not descend quite so low, but unfortunately not nearly enough, and a fast diminishing band.

With your permission we will take the report and accounts which have been in your hands for over the prescribed period as read.

The accounts show a deficit of $185,253.71 which at first sight may appear disappointing, but is not really so when you remember that in this, the first year, only pioneer work in building and developing could be done, as is always the case with such companies as this.

Our business may be divided into three sections

There is first, Kowloon Marine Lot No. 39, an open lot with no permanent buildings, the development of which was the original object for which the company was incorporated. At the time we bought it, it was bringing in a very small income and it was quite understood that it could not be made remunerative at the price we paid for it, which, with legal and other charges comes to $2,129,201. We are now receiving in storages about half what we pay out in interest on mortgage, and although these rents are still increasing, we cannot, of course, expect to cover the full interest without further capital expenditure. The site is a very valuable one situated immediately adjoining the Yaumati Police Station, and our present idea is to develop it with first-class Chinese houses and banking premises for which there is a demand on the back portion of the lot, leaving the front portion with the marine and pier rights for storage purposes.

The second section comprises Marine Lot No 286 known as "St. George's" Building. This was acquired last January, but we could not enter into possession until August, and, of course, the rents under the old leases leave a deficit after payment of interest. Some of the old leases have since run out, and by next October every one of them will have expired and the new rents that have been agreed upon will leave us a fair return on our investment.

The third section covers the Remaining Portion of Sec. A of Inland Lot 905 and Sub-section I of Sec. A of Inland Lot 905 known as the Kennedy Town property on which we began to build the moment we came into possession, and we are now just completing a block of 37 four-storeyed Chinese dwelling houses and shops for which there is a strong demand in that neighbourhood and which we estimate will bring us a net return of seven per cent. on our outlay.

Now with regard to finance so far we have called up only one half of the subscribed capital, i.e., $500,000, and the remaining half is not due till July 15 this year. headline: WHY SKY IS BLUE. / LIGHT SCATTERED BY MOLECULES.
text:
Why the sky is blue was explained by Sir Ernest Rutherford, when, in the theatre of the Royal Institution, he delivered the second of his course of four lectures on "The Counting of Atoms." He explained that the incessant movement of minute particles was first observed by an Englishman named Brown in 1827 and was now called the Brownian movement. It is now known that this constant agitation is a necessary consequence of the invisible and irregular movements of the molecules of the surrounding fluid, to be expected on the kinetic theory of matter. Examples of this Brownian movement shown by minute colloidal particles viewed through a high-power microscope were illustrated in a striking way by a cinematographic film. The behaviour of a large number of equal spheres, obtained from an emulsion of gum arabic or mastic was carefully examined by Perrin. He showed that they behaved in exactly the same way as an atmosphere of molecules of very great size and weight, and that the concentration of particles with height fell off according to the same law as an isothermal atmosphere. Knowing the mass and radii of the drops, he was able to deduce from the distribution of particles the Avogadro constant for a gas, thus fixing the number of molecules in a known weight of matter. About the same number was also deduced from the actual movement of individual drops, and from the rate of rotation of a large selected drop showing that the equipartition of energy held for large particles as well as for a gas. Finally, the Brownian movement of a small oil drop in air has been accurately measured by Fletcher, and has given a very concordant value for the Avogadro constant. These experiments had, in addition to serving as a method of counting the molecules, given a complete verification of the kinetic theory of gases, so the speed and number of collisions a molecule makes per second can be estimated with certainty.

An account was then given of the late Lord Rayleigh's theory of the blue of the sky, which was ascribed to the scattering of the light of the sun by the molecules of air in its path. This scattering is analogous to the scattering of light by fine particles, shown long ago by Tyndall at the Royal Institution. Experiments were shown to illustrate the polarisation of light by liquids and gases containing fine particles in suspension, and the cause of the red sunset. The present Lord Rayleigh, and afterwards Cabannes, showed experimentally that this scattering of light by gases could be measured in the laboratory. The variation of the intensity of the sun's light at different zenith distances gives an actual measure of this scattered light, and from this the number of molecules in a cubic content of air can be directly deduced. This value is in good accord with other data.

Meudon, a little town in the Paris suburbs, noted for its beautiful woods, has just had a curious strike. There was an election for the Municipal Council, but there were no candidates and no electors. Such unanimity is rarely seen. Nobody broke the tacit understanding of abstaining from the polls. The reason is that it was proposed by Paris, against the wish of the inhabitants, to impose upon them an installation they did not desire. Thereupon the Council resigned in protest, and the townsfolk unanimously abstained from voting. What is more, Meudon has by these tactics managed to win its way, and the objectionable proposal is withdrawn. It is now to be presumed that candidates will present themselves for the Municipal Council and that the inhabitants will vote for them.

In order to encourage the farmers of eastern Ontario in better breeding of live stock, the Canadian Pacific Railway is operating a Better Farming Special Train over its Ottawa-Pembroke branch. headline: SAME COLOUR / FRAMWAY TICKET / "SERIOUS OFFENCE."
text:
At the Central Magistracy this morning, before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, a Chinese named H. F. Cheune was charged with evading payment of tramway fare.

Mr. J. H. Simmons, traffic inspector of the Tramway Company, stated in evidence that he boarded car No. 34, proceeding east, near the Wing On Company on the afternoon of May 17. On asking accused to show his ticket, he said that he had a monthly ticket and later took out his purse in which was a ticket, only a part of which was visible. On examination witness found that the ticket was one issued for January 1923 and was of the same colour as those issued for the current month. On pointing out that the ticket was an old one, accused claimed to have left the ticket for May at home. Witness asked him to pay the fare, but accused quibbled about having no small change and later admitted he had no money. Accused then left the car, but he was later traced by the address given in the application for monthly ticket. Witness added that the last time accused held a monthly ticket was in March last year.

'Accused denied that he told the witness that he had left his ticket at home and admitted that he did not have one. He said that on the day in question he changed his clothing and his wife inadvertently put into his pocket an empty purse. His Worship said that it was clear to him that accused was guilty. His offence was serious one, but under the Tranway Ordinance there was provision for a fine only and His Worship would impose the maximum of $10.

The effect of the present Canadian immigration policy in encouraging farmers, farm labourers, and female household workers to come to Canada is indicated by a recent analysis according to occupation of immigrants arriving in Canada since 1920. In 1920 32 per cent. of the total immigration were agriculturists and, domestics, and in 1921 35 per cent. Since then the ratio of agriculturists and domestics toward all immigration has been steadily increasing, being 44 per cent. for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1923, 47 per cent. for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1924; and 51 per cent. for the nine months April to December inclusive of 1924. In these nine months the total immigration to Canada was 100,570, of which agriculturists and domestics represented 51,056.

headline: EROS IN PINK TIGHTS.
text:
An amusing rag by students took place in Cambridge on March 9 in connection with collection on behalf of the first pickers in Wisbech district.

A pyramid 30ft. high had been erected in the centre of the square with the apex veiled. King Henry VIII, attended by Cardinal Wolsey, pulled a cord which released the wrappings, and there poised on one foot was Eros.

Sitting at the foot of the monument were real flower sellers imported from Piccadilly for the occasion. They did not recognise their Eros, for the famous statue was being impersonated by the heaviest man in the University, who is well known as a weight putter. He was dressed in pink tights and red bathing costume, with wings complete. It was bitterly cold, and to add to his discomfort oranges were rained at him from all angles. As compensation, somebody climbed the pyramid with a bottle of beer.

FEAR FOR FRONTIER~The Poles are said to be disturbed over the German suggestion that part of Polish Pomerania be returned to Germany. Opposed to submitting the question to the league of nations, Poland will speedily place herself on a war footing.
